lead: This unit turns a square matrix into its eigenvalues, eigenvectors, and a diagonal form when one exists. After it you can compute characteristic and minimal polynomials, test diagonalizability, orthogonally diagonalize a real symmetric matrix, reduce a quadratic form to canonical form, and classify it and its conic by rank, index, signature, and definiteness.
about: Unit 4 starts with the characteristic polynomial and eigenvectors (4.1), then collects the shortcut properties and multiplicity facts (4.2). Cayley-Hamilton and the minimal polynomial (4.3) give a polynomial handle on a matrix. Similarity leads to the diagonalization test (4.4): enough independent eigenvectors. The advanced section (4.5) adds the spectral theorem for real symmetric matrices. Quadratic forms (4.6) use these diagonalizations to remove cross terms, and the final chapter (4.7) reads rank, index, signature, definiteness and conic type from the canonical coefficients. Each chapter uses small matrices so the arithmetic stays visible.

chapters.idea: The equation det(A − λI) = 0 produces the eigenvalues, and the nonzero null-space vectors of A − λI are the eigenvectors.
chapters.depth: Define characteristic polynomial, characteristic equation, eigenvalues and eigenvectors over R and C. Use det(A − λI) or det(λI − A); state the sign convention once. Compute 2×2 and 3×3 examples. Treat the eigenspace as the null space of A − λI. Introduce algebraic multiplicity. Read eigenvalues directly from triangular and diagonal matrices. Some syllabi call eigenvalues latent roots and eigenvectors latent vectors. Keep proofs short; the focus is calculation and meaning.

figure.title: Eigenvalue flow
figure.aria: A flow from matrix A to A minus lambda I, the characteristic equation, eigenvalues, null space, and nonzero eigenvectors.

chapters.example: For A = [[4, 1], [2, 3]], find the characteristic polynomial, both eigenvalues, and one eigenvector for each eigenvalue.
chapters.trap: The zero vector is not an eigenvector; substitute each λ and solve (A − λI)x = 0. A different sign convention for the characteristic polynomial changes only an overall factor.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 determinants and systems of equations; Unit 2 null space.
chapters.leave: Rank and consistency to Unit 1; null-space dimension and bases to Unit 2; matrix representation of linear maps to Unit 3; inner products to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: Eigenvalues obey simple bookkeeping rules under trace, determinant, powers, inverses, polynomials, and similarity, while multiplicities control how many independent eigenvectors exist.
chapters.depth: Cover trace = sum of eigenvalues with algebraic multiplicity, determinant = product, eigenvalues of diagonal and triangular matrices, A^k, A^{-1}, and p(A). State that similar matrices have the same characteristic polynomial and eigenvalues. Give the standard special-matrix facts: orthogonal and unitary eigenvalues lie on the unit circle; Hermitian and real symmetric eigenvalues are real; skew-symmetric eigenvalues are purely imaginary or zero; normal matrices have orthogonal eigenvectors. Define algebraic and geometric multiplicity and state geometric multiplicity ≤ algebraic multiplicity. Show that distinct eigenvalues give independent eigenvectors.

figure.aria: A tree of eigenvalue properties: sum is trace, product is determinant, powers, inverses, and polynomials transform each eigenvalue.

chapters.example: A 2×2 matrix A has eigenvalues 2 and 5. Find tr(A), det(A), the eigenvalues of A², A⁻¹, and p(A) for p(t) = t² − 3t + 1.
chapters.trap: Trace and determinant give only the sum and product of eigenvalues, not the individual eigenvalues. Eigenvalues of A + B are not generally the sums of eigenvalues of A and B.
chapters.leave: Full spectral theorem and orthogonal diagonalization to 4.5; SVD to Unit 5; graph spectra are outside this unit.

chapters.idea: Every square matrix satisfies its characteristic polynomial, and the minimal polynomial is the lowest-degree monic polynomial that kills the matrix.
chapters.depth: State the Cayley-Hamilton theorem and verify it on 2×2 and 3×3 matrices. Some syllabi state it without proof; keep the proof optional. Use it to compute inverses and reduce high powers. Define annihilating polynomial and minimal polynomial. State that the minimal polynomial divides the characteristic polynomial and has the same roots. State the diagonalization criterion: diagonalizable over the field iff the minimal polynomial splits into distinct linear factors. Include simple examples where minimal polynomial differs from characteristic polynomial.

figure.title: Polynomial handle
figure.aria: Cayley-Hamilton connects a matrix to its characteristic polynomial and supports power reduction, inverse computation, and the minimal polynomial.

chapters.example: For A = [[1, 2], [0, 3]], verify the Cayley-Hamilton theorem and use it to find A⁻¹. State the minimal polynomial.
chapters.trap: Cayley-Hamilton gives p(A) = 0, the zero matrix, not p(λ) = 0 for every scalar λ. The minimal polynomial divides the characteristic polynomial but need not equal it.
chapters.leave: Proof of Cayley-Hamilton and general module theory to later courses; the full diagonalization test is developed in 4.4.

chapters.idea: Similar matrices represent the same linear map in different bases, and A is diagonalizable exactly when it has enough independent eigenvectors to form a basis.
chapters.depth: Define similarity B = P⁻¹AP and show invariance of characteristic polynomial, eigenvalues, trace, determinant, and rank. Prove that A is diagonalizable iff it has n linearly independent eigenvectors. Form P with eigenvectors as columns and D with matching eigenvalues on the diagonal. State the equivalent multiplicity condition: for every eigenvalue, algebraic multiplicity = geometric multiplicity. Note that distinct eigenvalues are sufficient but not necessary for diagonalizability. Include a defective matrix example. Some syllabi say diagonalisable and use regular eigenvalues for simple or distinct cases; follow the local definition.

figure.title: Diagonalization test
figure.aria: The test asks for n independent eigenvectors; if yes, form P and diagonal D, if no, the matrix is not diagonalizable.

chapters.example: Diagonalize A = [[4, 1], [2, 3]] by finding P and D with P⁻¹AP = D.
chapters.trap: Columns of P must be independent eigenvectors in the same order as the diagonal entries of D. A repeated eigenvalue may still be diagonalizable, but only if its geometric multiplicity is large enough.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 1 and 2; Unit 1 systems; Unit 3 change of basis.
chapters.leave: Orthogonal diagonalization to 4.5; SVD and QR to Unit 5; full change-of-basis theory to Unit 3.

chapters.idea: A real symmetric matrix has an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors, so it can be diagonalized by an orthogonal matrix.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this. State the spectral theorem for real symmetric matrices: eigenvalues are real; eigenvectors from different eigenspaces are orthogonal; there is an orthonormal eigenbasis. Build Q with orthonormal eigenvectors as columns, so QᵀQ = I and QᵀAQ = D. For a repeated eigenvalue, apply Gram-Schmidt inside its eigenspace. Keep the treatment shorter than the main chapters and concentrate on 2×2 and 3×3 calculations.

figure.title: Symmetric spectral theorem
figure.aria: For a real symmetric matrix, eigenvectors from different eigenspaces are orthogonal; normalizing them gives Q with Q transpose A Q diagonal.

chapters.example: Orthogonally diagonalize A = [[2, 1], [1, 2]]: find an orthogonal Q and a diagonal D with QᵀAQ = D.
chapters.trap: Normalize every eigenvector, and use Gram-Schmidt inside a repeated eigenspace. Independent eigenvectors are not enough here; Q must satisfy QᵀQ = I.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 1 and 4; Unit 5 inner products and Gram-Schmidt.
chapters.leave: General quadratic forms to 4.6; SVD to Unit 5; complex spectral theory to later courses.

chapters.idea: A quadratic form xᵀAx with symmetric A becomes a sum of squares after a suitable change of variables; orthogonal changes use the eigenvalues.
chapters.depth: Define a real quadratic form and its symmetric matrix. Show how coefficients map to the matrix: ax² + 2hxy + by² gives [[a, h], [h, b]]. Reduce by an orthogonal change x = Qy to λ₁y₁² + ⋯ + λₙyₙ². Also cover Lagrange or congruent reduction to a canonical sum of squares. Discuss the general second-degree equation ax² + 2hxy + by² + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0: rotation removes the xy term and translation removes linear terms. Some syllabi call the result canonical form or normal form.

figure.title: Canonical reduction
figure.aria: A quadratic form with symmetric matrix is reduced by an orthogonal change of variables to a sum of eigenvalue times squared new variables.

chapters.example: Reduce Q(x, y) = 2x² + 2xy + 2y² to canonical form by an orthogonal change of variables.
chapters.trap: For ax² + 2hxy + by², the matrix is [[a, h], [h, b]], not [[a, 2h], [2h, b]]. The change x = Qy must use the eigenvector columns in the same order as the eigenvalues.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 1, 4, and 5; Unit 5 orthogonality; basic coordinate geometry.
chapters.leave: Rank, index, signature and conic classification to 4.7; SVD to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: The signs of the coefficients in a canonical form give rank, index, signature and definiteness, which classify the quadratic form and its conic.
chapters.depth: Define rank r, index p as the number of positive squares, and signature p − q where q is the number of negative squares; some syllabi use the pair (p, q) instead, so state the convention. Include zero count z. State Sylvester's law of inertia: p and q do not change under nonsingular changes of variables. Classify positive definite, negative definite, positive semidefinite, negative semidefinite, and indefinite forms. Apply the signs to the general second-degree equation and classify conics: ellipse, hyperbola, parabola, pair of lines, or imaginary type. Include simple numerical examples and conic nature problems.

figure.title: Inertia and type
figure.aria: Canonical coefficients are split by sign into positive, negative, and zero counts, which give rank, index, signature and definiteness.

chapters.example: For Q(x, y, z) = x² + 4y² − z², find the rank, index, signature and definiteness using index = number of positive squares and signature = p − q. Also classify the conic x² + 4y² − 4 = 0.
chapters.trap: Index and signature conventions vary. Decide whether index counts positive squares and whether signature is p − q or the pair (p, q). Signs, not the sizes of coefficients, decide definiteness.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 6; basic conic sections and coordinate geometry.
chapters.leave: Full rotation and translation computations to 4.6; detailed proofs of Sylvester's law are optional here.
